title: Meta shocked by $25B fine after N.M. refused to join multistate settlement
gist: A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion, its largest fine ever, after a jury found nearly 44 million violations of state consumer protection law over more than a decade of deceiving users about data control, data misuse, misinformation and equal enforcement. New Mexico had declined to join Meta's $18 billion multistate settlement. Meta, which expected at most $3.4 billion, will appeal on constitutional grounds, while watchdogs urge states to scrutinize its AI assistant Muse.

themes.theme: Size and basis of the $25B penalty

insights.claim: US district court judge Francis J. Mathew ordered Meta to pay New Mexico $25 billion, the largest fine ever imposed on Meta, after a jury found nearly 44 million violations of state consumer protection laws. He said the trial record supported the highest penalty level allowed under the state's Unfair Practices Act.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: This is a large one-off liability for META and a precedent for state-level penalties far above federal settlements.
insights.quote: “The jury was unequivocal: Facebook systematically misled the public”

insights.claim: New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez declined to join the $18 billion settlement Meta reached earlier this year with attorneys general in nearly all states, then won $25 billion at trial after asking for up to $40 billion. Torrez argued that Meta would not change unless the penalty hurt its stock price.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Opting out of a multistate deal and going to trial paid off here, which may encourage other states to hold out on future tech settlements.

insights.claim: Meta expected to pay at most $3.4 billion and wanted New Mexico's penalty in line with its $5 billion FTC settlement over Cambridge Analytica. Judge Mathew said the FTC settlement "cannot be viewed in a vacuum" because past penalties and decrees had not deterred Meta's deceptive practices.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Courts may treat repeat offenses as grounds for escalating penalties, which raises the expected cost of future enforcement against big tech.

insights.claim: Meta's third-quarter earnings showed it paid close to $10 billion toward the multistate settlement; without that expense, its income from operations would have been $22 billion higher, according to a Verge report. Critics nonetheless call the New Mexico fine a "drop in the bucket" for a company making $200 billion a year.

insights.claim: The trial record showed that top Meta leadership, including Mark Zuckerberg, knew Facebook was making misleading public statements over more than 11 years. In one message Zuckerberg wrote: "Give them a chance to change their privacy settings but obviously don't encourage it."
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Evidence of executive knowledge makes the verdict harder to reverse on appeal and invites more litigation.
